en: The Sūtra on the Supreme Reliance Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One, translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Liang Dynasty.
Chapter One: Weighing Merit (Part One). Chapter One: Weighing Merit.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha, the Bhagavān, was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. All were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who had accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, and completely severed the fetters of existence; their minds were well-liberated and well-mastered, and they were well-versed in śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Their names were: the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Bhadrika, the Venerable... [and so forth].
Pāṭaliputra, the Venerable Mahānāma, the Venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa, the Venerable Gayākāśyapa, the Venerable Nadīkāśyapa, the Venerable Yaśoda,
the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Śāriputra, and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
The Venerable Subhūti, the Venerable Subhūti, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, the Venerable Upāli,
the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the Venerable Mahācunda, the Venerable Mahākapphiṇa, and the Venerable Revata.
The Venerable Pilindavatsa, the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Sundarananda,
and the Venerable Rāhula— with the exception of Ānanda, who was still on the stage of training—
there were one thousand two hundred and fifty such persons.
Furthermore, there was a community of five hundred great bhikṣuṇīs present together, whose names were:
the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, the bhikṣuṇī Citrā, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā, the bhikṣuṇī Nandā, and the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā; each of these had her own retinue.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the assembly of Bodhisattvas within this Bhadrakalpa, all of whom had thoroughly penetrated the profoundly deep nature of dharmas (dharmatā). Having been tamed, transformed, and guided through their practice of equality, they cultivated the Bodhisattva path and served as true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) to all sentient beings. Having attained unimpeded dhāraṇīs and turned the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma, they had already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas; they had all gathered from worlds in other directions, with the venerable Bodhisattva Maitreya, who is in his final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), as their leader.
Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of millions of upāsakas, with King Bimbisāra as their leader.
There were also immeasurable hundreds of thousands of upāsikās, with Queen Vaidehī as their leader.
At that time, the World-Honored One was being reverently honored, followed, and provided with offerings by all the devas and humans.

Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda, within the great assembly, relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!”

Today, having dressed and taken my bowl, I entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms in due order. I saw a certain place where a great, high, multi-storied pavilion had been newly completed, adorned with exquisite carvings and paintings, its interior and exterior perfectly detailed. Upon seeing this, a thought arose in my mind:
"If a faithful son or daughter of good family were to construct such a great, high, multi-storied pavilion and offer it to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, providing them with the four requisites;

and if, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, one were to take a Buddha-relic the size of a mustard seed and enshrine it in a stūpa as large as an āmalaka fruit, with a harmikā as large as a needle, a rain-pavilion as large as a jujube leaf, and a Buddha-image as large as a grain of wheat—of these two merits, which would be superior?"
"I now ask the World-Honored One; I only pray that you will explain this.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"

Ānanda! You are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a great matter; you are capable of practicing manifold benefits, showing compassion for the world as a place of refuge, enabling gods and humans to attain the peace and happiness of the Path, and uprooting sentient beings so they do not remain in the ground of suffering.
"Therefore, Ānanda! Listen now with close attention; contemplate it with focused mindfulness, and receive it with a reverent heart and faith.
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy," [said Ānanda]. The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"

This Jambudvīpa world is seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth; its northern border is vast, while its southern part is shaped like a chariot, and the faces of the people there are likewise. It is entirely filled with srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and others, as dense and without gaps as a grove of sugarcane, bamboo, or reeds, or a field of hemp or rice.
In this way, Ānanda!

Suppose this Jambudvīpa were filled with *srotāpannas* up to *pratyekabuddhas*, and a certain person were to provide them throughout their entire lives with robes, food and drink, medicinal requisites, and bedding; and after they had entered *parinirvāṇa*, were to erect great stūpas for all of them and make offerings of lamps, incense, unguents, powdered incense, flower garlands, robes, parasols, banners, and pennants.
"Ānanda! What do you think? By reason of these causes and conditions, would this person generate much merit? Ānanda replied:
“Very many, World-Honored One! Very many!”
"Sugata! By these causes and conditions, this person generates much merit.
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! Let us set aside Jambudvīpa for a moment.

In the western continent of Aparagoyānī, which is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth and shaped like a half-moon—with the faces of its inhabitants likewise so shaped—if it were filled with those from Srotāpannas up to Pratyekabuddhas, as densely packed as a grove of sugarcane, bamboo, or reeds, or a field of hemp or rice, leaving no empty space;”
In this way, Ānanda!

Suppose this continent of Aparagoyānī were entirely filled with *srotāpannas* up to *pratyekabuddhas*, and a certain person were to provide them throughout their entire lives with clothing, food and drink, medicinal requisites, and bedding; and after they had entered *nirvāṇa*, were to erect great stūpas for all of them and make offerings of lamps, incense, unguents, flower garlands, robes, parasols, banners, and pennants.
"Ānanda! What do you think? Based on these causes and conditions, would this person generate much merit? Ānanda replied:
“Very many, World-Honored One! Very many!”
"Sugata! Ānanda, let us set aside the continent of Aparagoyānī for now."

Pūrvavideha is nine thousand yojanas in length and breadth; its continent is circular like the full moon, and the faces of its people are likewise shaped. It is filled with *srotāpannas* up to *pratyekabuddhas*, as densely packed as a grove of sugarcane, bamboo, or reeds, or a field of hemp or rice, leaving no empty space.
In this way, Ānanda!

Suppose there were a person who, throughout their entire life, provided clothing, food and drink, medicinal requisites, and bedding to all those in Pūrvavideha—from those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry up to pratyekabuddhas—and after they had entered parinirvāṇa, built great stūpas for each of them and made offerings of lamps, burning incense, unguents, powdered incense, flower garlands, robes, parasols, banners, and pennants.
"Ānanda! What do you think? Based on these causes and conditions, would that person generate much merit? Ānanda replied:
“Very many, World-Honored One! Very many!”
"Sugata! "Ānanda! Let us set aside the continent of Pūrvavideha for now."

The northern continent of Uttarakuru is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth; the continent is square, and the faces of its inhabitants are likewise. It is filled with srotāpannas up to pratyekabuddhas, as densely packed as a grove of sugarcane, bamboo, or reeds, or a field of hemp or rice, leaving no empty space.
In this way, Ānanda!

Suppose this Uttarakuru were filled with *srotāpannas* up to *pratyekabuddhas*, and a certain person were to provide them throughout their entire lives with robes, food and drink, medicinal requisites, and bedding; and after they had entered *nirvāṇa*, were to erect great stūpas for all of them and make offerings of lamps, incense, unguents, powdered incense, flower garlands, robes, parasols, banners, and pennants.
"Ānanda, what do you think? By reason of this, would that person generate much merit? Ānanda replied:
“Very many, World-Honored One! Very many!”
"Sugata! "Ānanda! Let us set aside the continent of Uttarakuru for a moment."

In the celestial palace of Śakra, Lord of Devas, there is a great soaring pavilion named the Hall of Constant Victory (*Nitya-jaya*), surrounded by eighty-four thousand high towers. It has eighty-four thousand pillars of blue lapis lazuli, covered above by a net of pure gold jewels. Nets of golden cords and bells are spread on all four sides, while the ground is strewn with gold and silver sand, sandalwood scented water, and various kinds of celestial flowers. There are eighty-four thousand ornate windows, adorned with an intermingling of *vaiḍūrya* gems, *indranīla* gems, crystal gems, and lotus-colored gems. There are eighty-four thousand balustrades and stairways, composed entirely of blue lapis lazuli.

Ānanda! Suppose there were a faithful son or daughter of good family who constructed flying pavilions, high towers, and the eternally victorious jeweled palaces of Śakra’s celestial palace—hundreds of thousands of *koṭis* of them—and bestowed them upon the Saṅgha of the four quarters;

and suppose, furthermore, that after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, another person were to take a relic as small as a mustard seed and construct a stūpa as large as a *mālā* fruit, with a *yaṣṭi* (spire) as thin as a needle, a *cūḍikā* (umbrella) as small as a jujube leaf, and fashion an image of the Buddha as small as a grain of wheat. This merit, compared to what was previously described, does not equal even one hundredth part; it does not equal one ten-millionth, one billionth, nor even one *asaṃkhyeya* (incalculable) part. No fraction can reach it, and no analogy can express it.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is immeasurable, Ānanda!
Setting aside such merit for a moment:

suppose this Jambudvīpa, Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, and Uttarakuru; the great oceans, Mount Sumeru, and the Iron Ring Mountains; together with the Sahā world—all were ground into atoms. If one were to count these atoms in sequence, and if there were a faithful son or daughter of good family who, throughout their entire life, made offerings to as many *srotāpannas*, *sakṛdāgāmins*, *anāgāmins*, *arhats*, and *pratyekabuddhas* as there were atoms, or who, after their parinirvāṇa, raised stupas to make offerings to them.
"What do you think?
Would these sons or daughters of good family acquire much merit? "Very much."
"World-Honored One!
It is very much so. Sugata!"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there are sons or daughters of good family who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, take up relics as large as mustard seeds, construct stūpas as large as āmalaka fruits, erect *yaṣṭi* poles as large as needles, install *harmikā* domes as large as jujube leaves, and fashion images of the Buddha as large as barley grains—the merit of this does not equal even one hundredth of what was previously described; it does not equal one ten-millionth, one billionth, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy."

Ānanda! If this merit were not dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the mass of merit would yield a reward of blessings equal in number to the atoms within the entire Sahā world, such that one would become the king of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the king of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the king of the Tuṣita Heaven, the king of the Yāma Heaven, or the king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—not to mention becoming a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*).
**Chapter Two: The Tathāgata-dhātu (Part One)** *The Sūtra of the Supreme Reliance*, Chapter Two: The Tathāgata-dhātu. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:

“After the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Bhagavān, if one erects lands, establishes stūpas, and fashions images for veneration, the merit and karmic reward thereof are immeasurable; they cannot be known even by the calculation of motes of dust.”
Why is this so? Ānanda! The Tathāgata is rare and inconceivable.

Why is this? Because the realms and natures are inconceivable; because awakening and realization are inconceivable; because the qualities and dharmas are inconceivable; and because the benefits and activities are inconceivable.
Ānanda! What is the realm of the Tathāgata?
In what way is the realm of the Tathāgata inconceivable?

Ānanda! All sentient beings possess the aggregates, sense bases, and elements; their superior characteristics and types manifest internally and externally, having flowed in continuous succession from beginningless time, obtained through the very nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as something most luminous, wondrous, and virtuous.

In this state, if mind, intellect, and consciousness cannot arise through conditions, if applied and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra) and discrimination cannot arise, and if improper mental attention (ayoniśo-manasikāra) cannot arise;
if one is separated from improper mental attention, these phenomena do not give rise to ignorance;
and if ignorance does not arise, these phenomena are not the conditions for the arising of the twelve links of existence (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda).
If it were not the condition for the arising of the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), this dharma would be without characteristics (*animitta*).

If it were without characteristics, this dharma would be unconditioned, neither arising nor ceasing, neither diminishing nor exhausting; it would be eternal, constant, quiescent, and abiding. Its intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) is pure, free from defilement and attachment, remote and stainless. It has transcended the shell of afflictions (*kleśakośa*) into liberation, is in perfect accord with the Dharma of the Tathāgata, and is inseparable from, never forsaken by, and inconceivable in its wisdom—surpassing that which exceeds the sands of the Ganges.

Ānanda! It is like a priceless wish-fulfilling jewel, adorned, polished, lovely, bright, and pure; its substance is perfectly clean and free from any stain or impurity, yet it has been cast away in foul mud for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.

After this has passed, someone picks it up; having picked it up, they wash it clean and preserve it with care so that it does not fall. Once this wish-fulfilling gem has been washed and maintained, it regains its purity without losing its precious nature.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
When all Tathāgatas were formerly on the causal ground, they knew that the nature of the realm of sentient beings is inherently pure, yet defiled by adventitious afflictions.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, reflect thus: "The adventitious afflictions do not enter the pure realm of sentient beings;

these stains of affliction are external obstructions and coverings, constructed by false conceptualization. We are able, for the sake of all sentient beings, to preach the profound and wondrous Dharma to eliminate the obstacles of affliction. One should not give rise to an inferior mind; because of one's vast capacity, one should conceive a heart of respect toward all sentient beings, engender reverence for the Great Teacher, engender *prajñā*, engender *jñāna*, and engender great compassion. By relying on these five dharmas, a bodhisattva attains the stage of *avaivartika*."
These bodhisattvas further reflected:

"These defilements are powerless and incapable; they do not correspond with a root, they have no true root, no basis, and no fundamental source. Their fundamental nature is most pure; therefore, they have no root."

False conceptualization arises from inverted habitual tendencies; just as earth, water, and wind abide by depending upon their respective bases, yet these bases themselves have no further basis, so too are the afflictions: they have no true basis.
If one knows correctly and contemplates with right reflection, these afflictions will not arise in opposition.
I should now contemplate so that the afflictions do not defile me; if there are afflictions that cannot defile me, this is called "excellent."
"If we ourselves were to be defiled by afflictions, how could we preach the Dharma for sentient beings to untie their bonds of affliction?
Therefore, we should now abandon afflictions and preach the True Dharma to untie the bonds of sentient beings."

If there are afflictions that cause the continuity of birth and death yet are associated with roots of goodness, such afflictions I should embrace, in order to bring sentient beings to maturity and to bring the Buddha-dharma to maturity.
"In this way, Ānanda!

When the Tathāgata was on the path of practice, relying on knowledge of reality as it is and relying on cultivation according to the measure of reality, he realized the realm of the Tathāgata—untainted and unattached—and was able to enter into and circulate within birth and death. Unbound by afflictions, he realized great skillful means, abiding in non-abiding, quiescent nirvāṇa, and swiftly attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

“Ānanda! This realm of the Tathāgata is immeasurable and boundless, yet it is concealed and obscured by the husks of all afflictions. Following the flow of birth and death, it drifts and sinks within the six realms, revolving without beginning; this I call the realm of sentient beings.”

Ānanda! Those beings within the realm of sentient beings who, having given rise to weary detachment toward the suffering of birth and death, eliminate the desires of the six sense objects, and rely upon the eighty-four thousand Dharma gates subsumed within the ten pāramitās to cultivate the path to bodhi—I call them bodhisattvas.

Ānanda! These beings in the realm of sentient beings have already emerged from the eggshell of all afflictions; having transcended all suffering and washed away all impurities, they are ultimately serene, pure, and limpid. They are the object of the aspiration of all beings, abiding in the subtle, supreme ground—the ground of omniscience—which is entirely unimpeded. Having entered this state and dwelt therein until reaching incomparable capability, and having attained the great sovereign power of the Dharma King, I call them Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
“Ānanda! This realm of the Tathāgata is equal in all respects throughout the three stages; it is entirely without obstruction, primordially quiescent.
It is like space, which cannot be covered, filled, or blocked by any kind of form—whether in an earthen vessel, a silver vessel, or a golden vessel, the space within them is equal.”
The Tathāgata-element is likewise so: throughout all three stages and in all places, it is entirely without obstruction. Ānanda!

When all Tathāgatas were on the causal ground, relying on knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) and practicing according to the measure of reality (*yathāmātra*), they contemplated the five kinds of merit of the Tathāgata-element. It is ineffable and non-dual in character; it transcends identity and difference, transcends the sphere of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), and is of a single flavor in all places.

Having seen this, the bodhisattva eliminates the notion of sentient beings, eliminates the notion of the distinctness of phenomena, and eliminates the notion of great fetters. Relying on unimpeded wisdom, he contemplates the *tathāgatadhātu* within the continuum of sentient beings and gives rise to a sense of wonder, thinking:
"Alas, sentient beings! The Tathāgata is right within the bodies of sentient beings, yet they do not see the Tathāgata according to reality."

Therefore, I speak of the complete holy path (āryamārga) which opens up and resolves the obstructions and veils of beginningless habitual tendencies (vāsanā). By the power of this holy path, all sentient beings may shatter these habitual tendencies and personally realize and perceive the true equality of the Tathāgata, in accordance with reality.
For what reason is this so?
All sentient beings are bound by their attachment to signs; they do not recognize the Tathāgata, do not attain the Tathāgata, and do not see the Tathāgata. Ānanda!

In the past, when the Tathāgata was on the path of practice, he contemplated the realm of the Tathāgata until he attained thorough and clear penetration; having realized that all dharmas are equal and such-like, he correctly turned the unsurpassed, subtle Dharma wheel, uprightly bringing the assembly of noble disciples to maturity, surrounded by immeasurable and boundless reverence, and abiding in the nirvana without remainder, cool and serene, never abandoning sentient beings for their benefit even until the end of the world.

“Ānanda! Because this realm of the Tathāgata is pure by its very nature, it possesses no marks of difference and no distinctions among sentient beings; it is perfectly conformable to equality, clear, limpid, and smooth, being most wondrous, supple, and virtuous, and is in harmony therewith.”
Ānanda! Just as the nature of the water element is inherently clear and moistening, and is able to gather, moisten, and cause all medicinal herbs, trees, and plants to grow; so it is, Ānanda!

All Buddhas, while on the stage of practice (caryā-bhūmi), cultivate roots of goodness based upon the Tathāgata-realm to benefit sentient beings; for this purpose, they enter the triple world and manifest birth, aging, sickness, and death. However, these sufferings of birth, aging, and so forth for these Bodhisattvas do not exist as ultimate reality.
Why is this? Because they have already seen the realm of the Tathāgata as it truly is. Ānanda!

For example, suppose there is a wealthy elder who has only one son, who is handsome, intelligent, and clever. The father cherishes, loves, and protects him, watching over him with a heart that never for a moment lets go.
This boy, being young and small, is fond of dancing and play; unaware, he stumbles and falls into a great, deep pit filled with filth and rotting corpses—a place of putrid stench.
The child’s mother and the other relatives, seeing their son fallen into the pit, cried out in alarm and wailed loudly, exclaiming, "Alas! What agony! What distress and anguish!
Although these kinsmen lamented with such grief, they were physically powerless and weak, unable to enter this deep pit to rescue their son from his suffering.
At that time, the elder quickly rushed back; with a heart heavy with concern for his son, he did not recoil from the foul stench as he entered the pit himself, seized his son, and pulled him out.
Thus it was, Ānanda!
I have employed this parable to reveal the true meaning: the corpse in the pit of excrement represents the triple world;
the one son represents ordinary sentient beings;

and the mother and her attendants represent the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—those of the two vehicles who, seeing all sentient beings drifting in the stream of existence and submerged in the cycle of birth and death, feel sorrow, lament, and compassion, yet lack the power and ability to rescue and deliver them.

The wealthy and noble elder is indeed a bodhisattva; with a mind that is pure, stainless, and free from defilement, having already been able to realize and see dharmas never before practiced, he enters the foul and evil realm of birth and death to manifest the assumption of a body for the sake of rescuing and delivering sentient beings.

Ānanda, you should know that such a bodhisattva’s great compassion is rare and ineffable; having transcended the triple world and liberated themselves from all fetters, they enter the triple world again to undergo birth within the three realms. By means of *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), they uphold the *prajñāpāramitā* (perfection of wisdom); thus, although they possess afflictions (*kleśa*), these cannot defile them, as they proclaim the true Dharma to extinguish the suffering of sentient beings.
Ānanda! You should know that this realm of the Tathāgata is characterized by great majestic power, immutability, and gentle suppleness. Ānanda!

This realm of sentient beings is the nature of all noble ones; it is neither cultivated nor uncultivated, neither practiced nor unpracticed, neither mind nor mental factors, neither karma nor retribution, neither suffering nor pleasure. To enter this state is to realize that this nature is equal, this nature is without differentiated marks, this nature is detached, this nature is compliant, this nature is vast, this nature is without "mine-ness," this nature is without high or low, this nature is true, this nature is inexhaustible, this nature is eternally abiding, and this nature is luminously pure.
Ānanda! What is this nature that is the nature of all noble ones?
It is because all noble dharmas are established by taking this as their condition, and all noble persons are manifested in dependence upon this nature, that I call it the nature of all noble ones.

“Ānanda! I now speak of the nature of the Tathāgata—the true reality unique to all Tathāgatas, exceeding the sands of the Ganges. It is from this Dharma that [all things] emerge and become manifest; it is called the realm of the Tathāgata.”

By having faith and delighting in the true teaching, and by cherishing and relishing its profound flavor, one immediately achieves the body of precepts, concentration, and wisdom of all noble and holy beings; for this reason, this Dharma is called the Dharmakāya.

These dharmas are mutually inclusive and not separate; they do not abandon wisdom, nor are they characterized by conceptual understanding. They are the reliance, the support, and the locus. If dharmas were not mutually inclusive, were separate, abandoned wisdom, or possessed conceptual understanding, they would likewise be the reliance, the support, and the locus. Therefore, I say that because all dharma-treasuries are unchanging, they are called *tathatā* (suchness); because they are free from inversion, they are called the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality); because they transcend all marks, they are called *śānti* (quiescence); and because they are the sphere of non-conceptual wisdom where the noble ones practice, they are called the *paramārtha* (ultimate truth).
Ānanda! This realm of the Tathāgata is neither existent nor non-existent, neither defiled nor pure; it is by nature stainless and conjoined with purity—you should know this!
“Ānanda! In what way is the Tathāgata’s realm inconceivable? Ānanda!”

This realm of the Tathāgata exists within the stage of defilement, wherein pure and impure dharmas coexist at one and the same time; this state is inconceivable and is attained through liberation based on the profound principle. It is not the domain of those who have become Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.
Ānanda! There are two kinds of dharmas that cannot be fully comprehended:
first, the intrinsically pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) cannot be fully comprehended; [and second, the tathāgatagarbha cannot be fully comprehended].
Second, because the defilements and hindrances are impenetrable, only non-regressive bodhisattvas who are in accord with the Great Dharma can hear, receive, and uphold it.
All bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas come to know this Dharma by virtue of their faith in the Buddha’s words.
Ānanda! For the Tathāgata, the nature of this realm is inconceivable.
Chapter 3: On Bodhi (Part One). *The Sūtra of the Supreme Reliance*, Chapter Three: On Bodhi. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"What is the Tathāgata’s anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"

The Buddhas, the Bhagavats, abide in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), where all obscurations are eternally exhausted, and their transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is tranquil, luminous, and pure.
You should know that this unsurpassed enlightenment is endowed with ten aspects.

What are the ten? First, intrinsic nature; second, causal conditions; third, afflictive hindrances; fourth, the attainment of the fruit; fifth, the performance of deeds; sixth, mutual inclusion; seventh, the sphere of activity; eighth, eternal abiding; ninth, non-commonality; and tenth, inconceivability.
“Ānanda! What is called the self-nature of bodhi?

It is the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) attained through practicing the path of renunciation according to principle and according to measure—the ten stages and the ten perfections—which is quiescent, luminous, and pure, and which lies beyond the sphere of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; this is precisely what is called the self-nature of bodhi.”
Ānanda! While this realm has not yet removed the shell of afflictions, I call it the Tathāgatagarbha, which is ultimately pure; this is called the basis for transformation.
It possesses four characteristics:

First, because it is the condition for arising; second, because it is the condition for cessation; third, because it is the fruit of the dharma known through correct maturation and reflection; and fourth, because it is the essence of the most pure dharma-realm.
What is called the condition for arising?
The continuous succession of all Tathāgatas throughout the world is the locus where the path to enlightenment arises as a condition.
What is called the condition for cessation?
Because the fundamental categories of the three grades of afflictions are eternally extinguished by relying upon and depending on this dharma.
What is the fruit of the knowable dharma?
It is because one has correctly and thoroughly realized the suchness of the knowable and attained its fruit.
What is called the essence of the dharma-realm?
It is because it is that which is manifested by the most pure dharma-realm, wherein all marks and fetters have been extinguished. Ānanda!

This is the characteristic of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); this transformation of the basis is the unsurpassed awakening of the Buddha, the Bhagavān, and is therefore called the nature of awakening (*bodhi-dhātu*). "Ānanda!
There are four kinds of dharmas that act as causes for attaining unsurpassed awakening."

What are these four? First, the aspiration to joyfully cultivate the Mahāyāna Dharma; second, the cultivation of the Prajñāpāramitā; third, the cultivation of the gateway to the Ākāśagarbha-samādhi; and fourth, the cultivation of the Tathāgata’s great compassion.
Ānanda! There are four kinds of delusions that obstruct the fruit of enlightenment. What are these four?

First, turning one's back on the Mahāyāna teachings; second, erroneously clinging to the view of a self; third, fearing the suffering of birth and death; and fourth, failing to perform deeds that benefit other sentient beings.
Ānanda! There are four kinds of unsurpassed, supreme fruits of enlightenment.
What are these four?
"First is supreme purity; second is the true self; third is wondrous bliss; and fourth is eternal abiding.

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, Ānanda rose from his seat amidst the assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, bowed low in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, spoke these verses:
"You who can teach and practice the most profound principle, Eternally crossing the stream of existence without falling back,"
Having transcended all enmities and fears, I therefore bow my head and inquire of Gautama:
What dharmas are the causes of bodhi?
What are called obstacles, and what is called the fruit?
"I only pray that the Honored One of benevolence and great compassion will take pity on us and explain it in detail.
At that time, the World-Honored One proclaimed:
"Excellent, Ānanda!"

You are able to inquire about the profound and great meaning of the Tathāgata; because you practice for the benefit of many sentient beings, so that humans and devas may attain the Way and find peace and happiness.
Now listen attentively, with a heart of yearning, reverence, and faithful acceptance.
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“In the world there are three classes of sentient beings:
first, those attached to existence; second, those attached to non-existence; and third, those who are neither attached to existence nor non-existence.
Those attached to existence are further divided into two kinds:”
First, they turn their backs on the path to nirvāṇa and lack the nature for nirvāṇa; they do not seek nirvāṇa but instead aspire to and delight in saṃsāra.
Second, they do not give rise to longing or reverence for my Dharma, but instead slander the Mahāyāna.
Ānanda! These beings are not disciples of the Buddha; the Buddha is neither their teacher nor their refuge.

Such people as these already dwell in ignorance and blindness; they will surely fall into the midst of perilous terrors and great darkness. In the wilderness, they further enter the dense forest of black filth and thorns; bound by birth and death until the end of time, they fall into the net of icchantikas and cannot escape on their own.
There are also two kinds of those who cling to non-existence:
first, those who practice the method of non-existence; second, those who practice the method of existence.
Regarding those who practice the method of non-existence, there are further two types of persons:
The first are the ninety-six kinds of heterodox practitioners outside the Buddha-dharma, such as the Cīrakāḥ, Pāṣaṇḍas, and so forth;
the second are those within the Buddha-dharma who are able to give rise to faith, yet stubbornly cling to the view of self and do not love the correct principle.
I say that such a person is the same as those non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, there are those with overweening pride who, while contemplating emptiness within the True Dharma, give rise to the dualistic views of existence and non-existence.

This true emptiness is the direct path toward unsurpassed bodhi, a single gate of pure liberation, which the Tathāgata has clearly revealed, opened, and correctly taught; yet if one gives rise to a view of emptiness within it, I say that such a person is incurable.
Ānanda! If there were someone who clung to the view of a self as large as Mount Sumeru, I would not be startled by it, nor would I condemn it;
yet, if a person of overweening pride were to cling to the view of emptiness as if it were a single hair divided into sixteen parts, I would not approve of that.
Regarding those who practice with skillful means, there are also two types:
first, those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, who cultivate only their own benefit and are unable to perform deeds for the benefit of others;
second, those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, who are slightly able to benefit others, yet abide in few activities and consider small gains to be sufficient.

Those who do not cling to existence or non-existence are those of the most superior faculties who practice the Mahāyāna; such persons do not cling to the *tathatā* (suchness) of saṃsāra, nor do they practice the *tathatā* of icchantikas which lacks skillful means, nor do they practice the *tathatā* of outsiders which possesses [only] skillful means. How, then, could the followers of the two vehicles practice?

Contemplating that the realms of birth-and-death and nirvana are equal and of a single characteristic, one attains the right path and the mind becomes stilled; abiding in the non-abiding pure nirvana, one wanders through birth-and-death without being defiled, taking the cultivation of great compassion as the foundation, with a resolute power so lofty and strong that it remains firm and immovable.
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
If a person is greedily attached to the three realms of existence and slanders the Mahāyāna, they are called an icchantika and fall into the category of those fixed in error.”
If a person clings to non-practice and lacks skillful means, they fall into the group of the indeterminate (aniyata-rāśi).

Furthermore, those who cling to non-practice while possessing skillful means, yet do not cling to the path of equality of both non-practice and practice, are called the group of the rightly determined (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi).
Ānanda! One who practices with equanimity, without clinging to existence or non-existence, is rare; setting this person aside, there are four other types:
first, the icchantika; second, the outsider; third, the śrāvaka; and fourth, the pratyekabuddha.
There are four afflictive obstacles that prevent one from realizing the unsurpassed bodhi of the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya. What are these four?
Abandoning the Mahāyāna is the obstacle of the icchantika;
To eliminate these obstacles, I teach that bodhisattvas practice with faith and joy in the true Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
The erroneous clinging to the view of a self in all circumstances is an obstacle of the non-Buddhists;
to eliminate this obstacle, I teach that bodhisattvas practice the dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā.
To feel weary, fearful, and exhausted within the cycle of birth and death is an obstacle for śrāvakas;
to eliminate this obstacle, I teach bodhisattvas the practice of the gateway to the Samādhi that Shatters Space.
Being content with minor acts of benefiting others is an obstacle for a Pratyekabuddha;
to eliminate this obstacle, I teach that Bodhisattvas practice great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

These four types of persons have four types of delusions; to eliminate these delusions, I teach the Four Noble Paths. By means of these superior paths, one remedies the four inversions and is able to realize the fruit of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, most wondrous Dharmakāya and its four virtues, the *pāramitās*.

“Ānanda! All phenomena such as form are entirely impermanent, yet one gives rise to the perception of permanence; all phenomena are suffering, yet one gives rise to the perception of pleasure; all phenomena are selfless, yet one gives rise to the perception of a self; all phenomena are impure, yet one gives rise to the perception of purity—this is called perversion.”
To contemplate that phenomena such as form are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure is not called a perversion;
however, if one contemplates the Tathāgata’s wondrously virtuous Dharma-body in this way, it constitutes a perversion.
To remedy these inversions, I speak of the four virtues of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body. What are the four?
First, the perfection of permanence; second, the perfection of bliss; third, the perfection of true self; and fourth, the perfection of purity.

Ānanda! All ordinary worldlings cling to the five internal aggregates and give rise to inverted views: they conceive the notion of permanence within the impermanent, the notion of pleasure within actual suffering, the notion of self within what is non-self, and the notion of purity within the impure.

Ānanda! Because the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is the sphere of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to observe the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body; thus, their inverted practices cannot be uprooted or severed.
Why is this so? One should cultivate the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya, which is supremely eternal, yet one turns away from cultivating the eternal and dwells in the cultivation of the impermanent;
one should cultivate the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya, which is the most sublime bliss, yet one turns away from cultivating sublime bliss and dwells in the cultivation of suffering.
One should practice the cultivation of the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya as the supreme true self, yet one practices by turning away from the true self and dwelling in the cultivation of non-self;
one should practice the cultivation of the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya as the most ultimate purity, yet one practices by turning away from purity and dwelling in the cultivation of impurity.

Therefore, one practices in reverse the path by which Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas abide; this is not the destination of the path of the four virtues of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body. Consequently, permanence, bliss, self, and purity are not within their realm.

Ānanda! If there are sentient beings who believe the words of the Tathāgata and are able to perceive the Dharma-body as permanent, blissful, self, and pure, these sentient beings will be free from inverted thoughts and give rise to true and correct vision.

Why is this so? Because the path in which Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas abide is practiced erroneously; it is not the destination of the path of the four virtues of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya. Therefore, the permanence, bliss, self, and purity of the Dharmakāya are not within their sphere of experience.

“Ānanda! If there are sentient beings who believe the words of the Tathāgata and are able to perceive the Dharma-body as permanent, blissful, self, and pure, these sentient beings will give rise to no perverted thoughts and will produce true and correct vision.”
Why is this so? Ānanda! The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is the perfection of true permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

If there are sentient beings who, by means of the supreme and wondrous path, contemplate the body of the Tathāgata, such beings pass from light into light and proceed from a state of peace and security to a place of supreme bliss. They are the true children of the Buddha, cherished by the Buddha’s heart; born from the Buddha’s mouth, they attain the Buddha’s accomplishments; and born through transformation from the Dharma, they receive their share of the Dharma-treasures.
Ānanda! Those who are icchantikas reject and turn their backs on the True Dharma, and with deep-seated craving, they take pleasure in the foul stench of birth and death.
To eliminate this delusion, I teach the practice of aspiring to and delighting in the Mahāyāna; by relying upon this Dharma, one attains the most pure fruit.

Ānanda! All non-Buddhists harbor false attachments and give rise to grasping based on the view of a self. Because the various phenomena such as form are characterized by selflessness and are free from contention, they are called the "True Self" throughout the three periods of time in all places, as well as in my own teaching.
These various non-Buddhists cling to the five internal aggregates and give rise to the view of a self, finding peace and happiness therein;
in order to destroy this delusion, I therefore teach the cultivation of the Prajñāpāramitā, for by relying on this dharma one attains the fruit of the true self.
Ānanda! Śrāvakas fear birth and death, and they find delight in the cessation of suffering;

to eliminate this attachment, I teach the cultivation of the gate of the Space-Shattering Samādhi. By relying on this Dharma, one attains the perfection of worldly and world-transcending bliss, the fruit of the pāramitās.

Ānanda! Those who are pratyekabuddhas are unable to contemplate the welfare of others; they do not dwell in harmony with sentient beings, but instead dwell alone in solitary reflection, their minds at peace and happy.

To eliminate this attachment, I teach the cultivation of the great compassion of a bodhisattva. By relying on this dharma, one constantly pervades the ten directions and remains to perform deeds for the benefit of all sentient beings; thus, one attains the fruit of the eternally abiding pāramitā.

Ānanda! By virtue of these four virtues, all Tathāgatas truly accord with the Dharma-realm; they do not cling to existence or non-existence, being like great empty space. Having cultivated the ultimate limit of the realm of emptiness, they abide eternally, transcending the three periods of time.
“Ānanda! All arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of the great stages, due to four kinds of obstructions, do not attain the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya and its four virtues of pāramitā.”
What are the four? First, the delusion that conditions birth; second, the delusion that causes birth; third, existence within existence; and fourth, non-existence.
What is the delusion that conditions birth?
That is to say, the dwelling of ignorance gives rise to all formative forces (*saṃskāra*), just as ignorance gives rise to karma.
What is the delusion that serves as the cause of birth?
It is the various formative forces produced by the Dwelling Place of Ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*), just like the various karmas produced by ignorance.
What is "existence within existence"?

It refers to the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) arising from outflow-free (*anāsrava*) formations, which have the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) as their condition and the ground of ignorance as their cause. This is analogous to how the three kinds of existence (*bhava*) arise, having the four graspings (*upādāna*) as their condition and the three kinds of outflowing karma (*āsrava-karma*) as their cause.
What is it that does not exist?

It is the imperceptible, subtle cessation occurring in dependence upon the three types of mind-made bodies, just as moment-to-moment aging and death occur in dependence upon the three realms of existence.

Because the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) serves as the basis for all afflictions and has not yet been severed, the Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and sovereign Bodhisattvas cannot attain the ultimate purification of the *pāramitā* that sees the total extinction of the foul stench of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the defilements of affliction.

Because delusions of subtle characteristics arise from the ground of the abiding of ignorance and false practices have not yet been eliminated, they cannot attain the ultimate great self (*mahātman*) *pāramitā* of supreme tranquility, which is without action and without practice.

Because outflow-free karma (*anāsrava-karma*) arises from the ground of the abiding of ignorance due to subtle falsehood, and the mind-born aggregates (*manomaya-skandha*) have not yet been exhausted, they cannot attain the ultimate bliss *pāramitā* of supreme cessation and detachment.

If one has not yet attained the permanent and complete exhaustion, without remainder, of all afflictions, karmas, and the difficulties of birth, then although these Tathāgatas are the realm of ambrosia (*amṛta-dhātu*), their death through transformation (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) remains to be severed, its flow extinguished, and its immeasurable [continuance] brought to an end; thus they cannot reach the vision of the ultimate, immutable, and great permanence that is the *pāramitā*.
“Ānanda! Within the three realms there are four kinds of difficulties:
first, the difficulty of afflictions; second, the difficulty of karma; third, the difficulty of retribution for birth; and fourth, the difficulty of faults.”
The *saṃskāra-bhava* (birth-and-death through effort) arising from the ground of ignorance is as difficult as the afflictions within the triple world;
the *hetu-pratyaya-bhava* (birth-and-death through causes and conditions) arising from the ground of ignorance is as difficult as karma within the triple world;
and the *bhava-bhava* (birth-and-death of existence) arising from the ground of ignorance is as difficult as birth within the triple world.
There is no birth-and-death arising from the ground of the abiding of ignorance, which is as difficult to overcome as the faults within the triple world.
It should be understood in this way, Ānanda!

Because the four kinds of birth and death have not yet been eliminated, the three types of mind-made bodies lack the perfections of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; you should know that only the Buddha’s Dharma-body is the perfection of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
“Ānanda! You should know that the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya, the great perfection of purity (viśuddhi-pāramitā), has two aspects:
natural purity is its universal characteristic, while stainless purity is its specific characteristic.”
It should be understood that the Great Self-pāramitā is of two kinds:
it is because it distances itself from all heterodox attachments to erroneous views and transcends the false notion of a self;
and it distances itself from the mistaken attachments of those of the Two Vehicles who rely on mere reasoning and transcends the false notion of non-self.
It should be known that the Great Bliss Pāramitā is of two kinds:
by severing the root of suffering and its accumulation and resolving the bonds of habitual tendencies, one is able to realize the cessation of all suffering;
for the mind-born aggregates have been completely uprooted.
It should be understood that the Great Constant Perfection (mahā-nitya-pāramitā) is of two kinds:
it does not diminish impermanent conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), for it transcends the view of nihilism;
nor does it augment eternally abiding nirvāṇa, for it transcends the view of eternalism.

If one calculates that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, this is called the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*); if one calculates that nirvāṇa is eternally abiding, this is called the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*).
To remedy the obstacles of the four delusions and overturn the four inversions, permanence, bliss, self, and purity constitute its true fruit.
“Ānanda! What are the matters that benefit awakening?
There are two such matters:”
The first is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and the second is subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom (*tatpṛṣṭhalabdha-nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
These two types of wisdom have two functions:
the first is for the accomplishment of one's own benefit (*svārtha*), and the second is for the accomplishment of the benefit of others (*parārtha*).
What is self-benefit?

To perfect the body of liberation and maintain the pure *dharmakāya*, thereby extinguishing the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and all cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), is called self-benefit;
non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is able to accomplish this dharma.
What constitutes benefiting others?

From the non-conceptual subsequent knowledge until the very end of the cycle of birth and death, one refrains from deliberate conceptualization; instead, one manifests the two bodies to teach the Dharma inexhaustibly, uninterruptedly, and immeasurably. This is for the sake of liberating beings from the sufferings of the three evil realms of birth and death, and for the purpose of establishing all sentient beings upon the good paths and causing them to abide in the stages of the Three Vehicles—this is called benefiting others.
Furthermore, self-benefit is inseparable from three aspects of merit:
first, the untainted (*anāsrava*); second, the pervasive (*vyāpin*); and third, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, benefiting others is inseparable from four aspects of merit, which rescue sentient beings so that they do not fall into the four states:

First, false views, delusion, and doubt; second, falling into the path of suffering, the evil paths, and the paths of ruin; third, destroying the true teaching with a mind of jealousy and a mind of enmity; and fourth, with an inferior mind, craving and delighting in the Lesser Vehicle.
Ānanda! To give rise to these two matters—benefiting oneself and benefiting others—is the work of bodhi.
“Ānanda! [he said.]
What are the dharmas associated with bodhi? Unsurpassed bodhi is the mark of reality, and nineteen kinds of dharmas are associated with it:

first, inconceivable; second, subtle; third, real; fourth, profoundly deep in principle; fifth, invisible; sixth, difficult to penetrate; seventh, eternal; eighth, existent; ninth, tranquil; tenth, constant; eleventh, cool; twelfth, pervasive; thirteenth, non-conceptual; fourteenth, unattached; fifteenth, unobstructed; sixteenth, compliant; seventeenth, ungraspable; eighteenth, great purity; nineteenth, clarity. These nineteen dharmas are never separated from unsurpassed bodhi; therefore, they are called the dharmas associated with bodhi.
“Ānanda! What is the sphere of activity for awakening?
Through three principles, the three bodies (trikāya) are manifested:”
First is the principle of profundity, second is the principle of vastness, and third is the principle of myriad virtues. Ānanda!
The first body is endowed with five kinds of characteristics and five kinds of merits.
What are the five characteristics?
First, the unconditioned; second, non-separation; third, freedom from the two extremes; fourth, liberation from all hindrances; and fifth, intrinsic purity.
What are the five kinds of merit?
First, immeasurability; second, incalculability; third, inconceivability; fourth, uniqueness; and fifth, ultimate purity.

The second body is manifested from the pure flow of the *dharmakāya*. With the immeasurable merits of all Tathāgatas as its attributes, and with *mahāprajñā* and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as its essence, it is endowed with five kinds of qualities:

first, the characteristic of non-conceptuality; second, effortlessness; third, performing benefit in accordance with the intentions of sentient beings; fourth, being inseparable from the *dharmakāya*; and fifth, constantly and universally remaining at all times without abandoning sentient beings.
The third body is manifested by the pure flow of *prajñā* and great compassion; its essence consists of the *rūpa*-skandha and it is endowed with fourfold qualities:
first, the thirty-two marks (*lakṣaṇa*); second, the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*); third, majestic power (*tejas*); and fourth, strength (*bala*).
It is capable of gathering in and corresponding to the faculties, desires, natures, and conducts of all sentient beings within the Buddha-field of impurity.
He manifests various Jātaka tales; or he manifests ascending to Tuṣita Heaven,
or manifesting descending from there, or manifesting entering the mother’s womb, or manifesting his initial birth from the womb,
or manifesting the stage of Kumāra, or manifesting his study of the eighteen vidyāsthānas.
Sometimes he manifests various playful activities while wandering in the rear gardens; sometimes he manifests leaving the household life or practicing asceticism;
sometimes he proceeds to the site of enlightenment or attains the Way of Buddhahood; sometimes he turns the wondrous Wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī;
or he enters parinirvāṇa in the Saṃkalpa Forest. He manifests such diverse matters as these, even unto the exhaustion of birth and death.
Regarding the future limit, Ānanda:
unsurpassed bodhi encompasses the three bodies in their entirety; therefore, it is called the sphere of activity of bodhi.
“Ānanda! What is the unexcelled bodhi that is the eternally abiding dharma?
This eternal abiding has two kinds of dharmas that act as its causes and conditions:”
First is non-arising and non-ceasing; second is being without end and without exhaustion. These are called the eternally abiding dharmas of bodhi. "Ānanda!
What are the unique characteristics of unsurpassed bodhi?
There are two kinds of non-commonality:
first, that which is unknowable, which ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas cannot penetrate as it is not within their sphere;
second, that which is unattainable, for no one except the Buddha alone can attain it.
These uncommon qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are of five kinds:

first, because the principle of suchness (*tathatā*) is profoundly deep; second, because sovereignty is unshakable; third, because they are subsumed within the pure, untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*); fourth, because they are unimpeded regarding all objects of knowledge (*jñeya-vastu*); and fifth, because they bring to perfection the benefit of sentient beings. These are called the uncommon characteristics of enlightenment (*bodhi*).
“Ānanda! What is this unsurpassed bodhi that is inconceivable?
There are six reasons why it is inconceivable:”

First, it transcends the realm of language; second, it is subsumed within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); third, it has already transcended the conceptualization and deliberation of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); fourth, it cannot be apprehended through analogies; fifth, it is the most supreme among all phenomena (*dharma*); and sixth, because it cannot be established as a location for either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa—it is called unsurpassed enlightenment that is inconceivable.
“Ānanda! In what way is the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed enlightenment inconceivable? Ānanda!”
All Tathāgatas abide in the state of unsurpassed enlightenment; therein, there are five kinds of inconceivable causes and conditions.
What are these five? First, self-nature; second, location; third, abiding; fourth, being one or different; and fifth, benefiting others.
Ānanda! Why is it that the Tathāgata’s own nature for awakening is inconceivable?
It is because the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended as form, nor can the Tathāgata be apprehended apart from form; and the same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The Tathāgata cannot be apprehended as the earth element, nor can the Tathāgata be apprehended apart from the earth element; it is the same for the water, fire, and wind elements.
The Tathāgata cannot be apprehended as the eye-entrance, nor can the Tathāgata be apprehended apart from the eye-entrance; it is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The Tathāgata cannot be apprehended as existent dharmas, nor is he so in the case of non-existent dharmas; this is called the inconceivable nature of bodhi.
Ānanda! How is it that the Tathāgata’s state of awakening is inconceivable?
The Tathāgata is inconceivable while in the desire realm, and he is also inconceivable when apart from the desire realm; it is likewise for the form and formless realms.
The Tathāgata is inconceivable among human beings, and he is also inconceivable apart from human beings; it is the same for the six realms of existence.

The Tathāgata is inconceivable in the eastern direction, and he is also inconceivable apart from the eastern direction; it is the same for all ten directions. This is called the inconceivability of location.
Ānanda! What is this inconceivable state in which the Tathāgata abides for the sake of awakening? Ānanda!

The Tathāgata’s dwelling in the abode of peace and bliss is inconceivable; the Tathāgata’s dwelling in the abode of tranquility is inconceivable; the Tathāgata’s dwelling with a mind is inconceivable; the Tathāgata’s dwelling without a mind is inconceivable; likewise, the Tathāgata’s dwelling in the Brahma-abodes and the noble abodes is inconceivable—this is called the inconceivability of the dwelling.
Ānanda! How is it that the Tathāgata is inconceivable as being either one or many?
The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time abide in a single place.
What is this single locus?
It is the naturally pure, untainted *dharmadhātu* of all Tathāgatas; whether they are one or many is inconceivable, and this is called the "inconceivability of oneness and difference."
Ānanda! How is it that the Tathāgata’s acts for the benefit of others are inconceivable?

In this way, the Tathāgatas are equal to the single Dharma-realm; their wisdom, spiritual power, right effort, and majestic virtue are all entirely equal. Abiding in the untainted, pure Dharma-realm, the Tathāgatas, through this transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), are able to bring immeasurable benefit to sentient beings; this is called the inconceivability of benefit.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of the inconceivable:
first, it is ineffable, because it transcends the realm of language;
second, it is beyond all worlds, because there is nothing in the world that can serve as an analogy for it. This is called the inconceivable.
Furthermore, True Suchness is fundamentally unstained and ultimately free from defilement;
it is inconceivable. Ānanda! This is called the inconceivability of Bodhi.

Chapter Four: The Qualities of the Tathāgata (Part Two). Chapter Four: The Qualities of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
“There are one hundred and eighty unique qualities; these are the supreme and wondrous merits of the Tathāgata.”
First, the thirty-two marks; second, the eighty secondary characteristics; third, the sixty-eight dharmas.
What are the thirty-two marks?
The Bodhisattva cultivates four causal conditions:
First is upholding the precepts; second is meditative concentration; third is patience; and fourth is relinquishing wealth and all afflictions.
By cultivating these four causes with firm and unshakable resolve, one attains two marks through these karmic conditions:
first, the soles of the feet are level and full, such that the ground upon which they tread becomes entirely even, so that the Bodhisattva’s feet are said to have no pits or hollows.
Second, his gait is level and even, without any slanting or crookedness.

If a bodhisattva makes various offerings to his parents, teachers, and elders, and provides various forms of relief to sentient beings suffering in hardship, performing these deeds diligently whether coming or going, through these karmic conditions he attains the mark of wheels on the soles of his feet, complete with hubs, rims, and adorned with a thousand spokes.

If a bodhisattva does not oppress or afflict others, refrains from theft, does not give rise to covetousness or seizure upon seeing what others cherish, does not boast of himself and eliminates arrogance, and toward teachers and elders rises to greet them, inquires after their well-being, stands in attendance, looks upon them with reverence, and joins his palms in respect—by these karmic conditions, he obtains two marks:
first, his fingers are slender, long, straight, and have sunken joints;
second, his body is broad, large, upright, and majestic.

By virtue of having fulfilled the three aforementioned causes and conditions of karma, one obtains long heels; by further practicing the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and performing deeds that benefit others through those three types of karma, one’s ten fingers and toes become webbed like those of a king of geese due to these karmic conditions.

If a bodhisattva assists and serves their teachers, parents, and elders—personally applying medicinal oils and ointments, massaging them, bathing them, providing clothing and food, and attending to their needs—they will attain hands and feet that are soft, supple, moist, and smooth, with palms as beautifully red as the lotus flower.
If a bodhisattva cultivates all wholesome dharmas with a mind free from weariness, increasing them ever further, they obtain full and rounded ankles.

If a bodhisattva studies the True Dharma and expounds it for others, traveling back and forth to teach and transform beings without becoming exhausted, through these karmic conditions they obtain calves like those of a deer king.

If a bodhisattva diligently seeks to know dharmas not yet attained and transforms and converts others through dharmas already attained; if they sever and block the three types of evil karma so that they do not arise; if their body and mind are not defiled by the evil dharmas of the six sense-objects; and if they bestow medicinal decoctions upon those with physical ailments and act as a skilled physician for those with mental ailments—by virtue of these karmic conditions, they obtain a body that is upright.

If a bodhisattva provides protection for those who are terrified, gives clothing and food to the poor and naked, and constantly maintains a sense of shame and remorse to prevent the arising of evil, through these karmic conditions he attains the mark of the sheathed male organ.

If a bodhisattva guards body, speech, and mind, constantly keeping them pure; if they receive offerings with contentment and know the proper measure in their use; if they give medicine to the sick and wealth to the poor; and if there are sentient beings whose karma is uneven, such that even their enjoyments are uneven, he exhorts them to practice deeds of equanimity. By virtue of these karmic conditions, he attains a body that is perfectly proportioned, with its length and girth equal like those of a nyagrodha tree.

If a bodhisattva skillfully practices various superior wholesome dharmas through expedient means, ensuring they never fall into middling or inferior grades but always cause them to increase, by virtue of these karmic conditions, he attains the mark of body hairs that point upward and curl to the right.

If a bodhisattva is by nature of sharp faculties and frequently contemplates the meaning of the teachings; if they draw near to the wise and encounter virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra); if they sweep and cleanse the dwellings of their elders and superiors, wash and massage their bodies, and remove filth from caityas; and if they do not allow adventitious afflictions (āgantukakleśa) to defile their minds—by the causal conditions of these deeds, they obtain a single hair per pore and skin that is fine, smooth, and impervious to dust and water.

If a bodhisattva joyfully gives away clothing, food and drink, vehicles, bedding, and various articles of adornment, with a mind free from regret or stinginess, through the causal conditions of this karma, they obtain a golden-colored body with a halo one fathom in width.

If a bodhisattva extensively bestows soft and delicious food and drink without limit, causing many sentient beings to all obtain full satisfaction, through the causal conditions of this karma, they attain the seven parts of the body being full and rounded.

If a bodhisattva sees virtuous beings wishing to cultivate wholesome dharmas, he acts as their honored guide by aligning his own actions with theirs, establishing them in goodness and severing all unwholesome deeds; through these karmic conditions, he attains the lion’s chest.

If a bodhisattva practices the four right endeavors for the sake of benefiting sentient beings among them, with a mind free from fear like that of a lion king, through these karmic conditions he attains two marks:

first, his two shoulders are level and even, and the areas beneath both armpits are full; second, his two arms are rounded and straight like the trunks of elephant kings, extending past his knees when held upright.

If a bodhisattva abandons the karma of divisive speech, brings about reconciliation among those who harbor enmity and resentment, practices the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather in sentient beings, contemplates profound meanings, and cultivates impartial compassion, through these karmic conditions they obtain two marks:
first, forty teeth in the mouth that are even, closely set without gaps, and white like jade or snow; second, the mark of four canine teeth that resemble the crescent of the new moon.

If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who have needs or desires and bestows upon them, according to their wishes, either material wealth or the Dharma, through the causal conditions of this karma they obtain two marks:
first, a lion-like jaw; second, a neck that is full and pure.

If a bodhisattva protects sentient beings as if looking upon an only son, giving rise to abundant faith and immeasurable compassion, and extensively bestows medicine and remedies with a mind free from impurity or turbidity, through these karmic conditions he attains two marks:

first, his throat is endowed with a thousand vessels, which receive delicious flavors and are moistened by flowing essences; second, the bones of his body are linked like a chain, as firm as those of Nārāyaṇa.

If a bodhisattva personally practices the ten wholesome paths of action and teaches others to practice them, rejoices and praises those who do so, possesses immeasurable great compassion and pities sentient beings, and gives rise to the mind of great vows to embrace the True Dharma, through these karmic conditions he attains two marks:
first, a *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of his head that rises up naturally to form a topknot; second, a tongue that is broad, thin, and long like a lotus petal.

If a bodhisattva constantly speaks truthful words, loving words, and beautiful words, expounding the true Dharma without error, by virtue of these karmic conditions, they obtain a Brahma-voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird, with a wondrous resonance as deep and far-reaching as the vibration of a celestial drum.

If a bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of loving-kindness and reverence, viewing all worlds as if they were their own father or mother, and regards all sentient beings without giving rise to the three poisons, through these karmic conditions they obtain two marks:
first, the eyelids are a beautiful blue like the *utpala* flower; second, the eyelashes are a deep azure radiance, like those of a bull king.

If a bodhisattva sees virtuous beings practicing the three trainings and praises their excellence without giving rise to disparagement, and upon seeing those who slander them, restrains and protects them—by these karmic conditions, they attain the mark of the white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa), which curls to the right and slopes upward between the eyebrows.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
By practicing four kinds of right action, a bodhisattva attains the thirty-two marks:
first, being resolute and free from confusion; second, observing with subtle and profound discernment; third, practicing constantly without interruption; and fourth, acting without inversion."
By the first karmic condition, one obtains soles that are level and full. By the second karmic condition, one obtains nine marks:

first, the mark of wheels on the soles of the feet; second, the fullness and roundness of the ankles; third, the dense webbing between the ten fingers and toes; fourth, skin that is fine and soft; fifth, the fullness of the seven locations; sixth, the evenness of the two shoulders and the fullness of the areas beneath both armpits; seventh, arms that are rounded and muscular; eighth, a broad and long tongue; and ninth, a chest like that of a lion.
Through the third karmic condition, five marks are obtained:
first, slender and long fingers; second, long heels; third, an upright body that is not crooked; fourth, equal proportions in both horizontal and vertical dimensions; and fifth, a full and pure neck.
The fourth karmic condition for attaining the remaining marks:
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If all sentient beings in the ten directions were to collectively practice the ten wholesome paths, and if such merit were increased a hundredfold, by virtue of this karmic condition, they would attain but a single pore-mark of a Bodhisattva."
When one enters into all the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), the merit increases a hundredfold more than before, and only then can one attain a single minor mark of a Bodhisattva.
When one enters into all the major marks (*lakṣaṇa*), the merit increases a hundredfold more than before, and only then can one attain a single major mark of a Bodhisattva.

Entering into all marks of merit, one is initially free from the mark of the ūrṇā-kośa and the mark of the uṣṇīṣa; when these merits increase a hundredfold, one attains the mark of the ūrṇā-kośa, and with another hundredfold increase, one attains the mark of the uṣṇīṣa.

Upon entering the *ūrṇā-kośa*, his merit increases a thousandfold; he attains the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) subsumed under the Tathāgata’s uncommon quality of the conch-shell [voice], and by virtue of these marks and signs, a single sound of the Tathāgata pervades the infinite worlds of the ten directions.
Ānanda! These thirty-two marks have three inconceivable causes and conditions:
first, the inconceivability of the time, for the cultivation [of the practices] was completed over the full span of three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
Second, the delight of the mind is inconceivable, because it seeks the peace, happiness, and benefit of all sentient beings;
third, the categories [of practice] are inconceivable, for one cultivates all that is wholesome and abandons all that is unwholesome, and these types of practice are inexhaustible.
Therefore, the Tathāgata’s body is endowed with inconceivable marks and secondary characteristics. "Ānanda!

“Ānanda! The Tathāgata possesses ten powers. What are these ten?

First is the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible; second is the power of knowing the ripening of karma; third is the power of knowing meditative concentrations and their categories; fourth is the power of knowing the degrees of the faculties; fifth is the power of knowing inclinations and interests; sixth is the power of knowing the various dispositions of beings; seventh is the power of knowing the paths leading to all destinations; eighth is the power of knowing past lives; ninth is the power of knowing death and rebirth; tenth is the power of knowing the exhaustion of the outflows.”
By means of this power of wisdom, the Tathāgata proclaims the most supreme and excellent state, turns the unsurpassed, pure Brahma-wheel, and lets out the true lion’s roar amidst the great assembly.
“Ānanda! The Tathāgata possesses four kinds of fearlessness: first, fearlessness regarding all-knowledge;

second, fearlessness regarding the destruction of the outflows; third, fearlessness regarding the proclamation of obstacles to the path; and fourth, fearlessness regarding the proclamation of the path leading to the end of suffering.”
“Ānanda! The Tathāgata has three kinds of foundations of mindfulness:
first, right mindfulness regarding right conduct; second, right mindfulness regarding wrong conduct; and third, right mindfulness regarding mixed conduct.”
Ānanda! The Tathāgata further possesses the dharma of great compassion. Ānanda!
The Tathāgata possesses eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*):

first, no fault in body; second, no fault in speech; third, no fault in mind; fourth, no lack of concentration; fifth, no attachment to diverse characteristics; sixth, no relinquishing through lack of knowledge; seventh, no diminution of aspiration; eighth, no diminution of right diligence; ninth, no diminution of mindfulness; tenth, no diminution of wisdom.

Eleventh, no decline in the liberations; twelfth, no decline in the knowledge and vision of liberation; thirteenth, bodily actions follow wisdom; fourteenth, verbal actions follow wisdom; fifteenth, mental actions follow wisdom; sixteenth, perfection of knowledge regarding the past; seventeenth, perfection of knowledge regarding the present; eighteenth, perfection of knowledge regarding the future.
“Ānanda! Only the Tathāgata has attained the swift supernormal power of mastery at will; only the Tathāgata has attained the supernormal power of transformation that is without limit;

The Tathāgata alone has attained mastery over the dharma of mental sovereignty; the Tathāgata alone has attained mastery in the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, which is infinite;

the Tathāgata alone knows the various distinctions among sentient beings in the formless realm; and the Tathāgata alone has attained thorough penetration regarding the parinirvāṇa of the noble assembly.
