"Ānanda! Briefly stated, the merits of the Tathāgata are of six kinds:
First, being complete; second, being stainless; third, being immovable; fourth, being unimpeded; fifth, benefiting others; and sixth, possessing mastery and skillful means.
Ānanda! How is it that the Tathāgata’s merit is inconceivable?

The boundless merit of all Tathāgatas throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—whether abiding in the stage of delusion or the stage of purity—is mutually inclusive and harmonious, never separated; it is neither defiled nor pure, and is thus inconceivable.
Chapter Five: On the Deeds of the Tathāgata (Part Two) The Sūtra on the Supreme Reliance, Chapter Five: On the Deeds of the Tathāgata “Ānanda! There are eighteen deeds of the Tathāgata;
they are peerless, most wondrous, supreme, and unsurpassed by any other, causing all sentient beings to give rise to a sense of wonder and to offer them reverence and worship. This is the first deed.
It is through the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics that [the body] is brought to perfection; the Tathāgata has realized cause and effect according to reality.
If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas propound the non-existence of cause and effect, or propound doctrines of unequal cause and effect, I shall immediately subdue them and cause them to fall into defeat;
this is the second matter.

It is by means of this power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible that the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision is perfected: he knows that one experiences the results of one's own karma, and that there is no such thing as one person performing an action while another receives its fruit.

If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas propound false doctrines and erroneous teachings concerning the transference of karma or the transference of its reception, the Tathāgata is able to subdue them and cause them to fall into defeat;
this is the third matter.

Through the attainment of the power of knowledge regarding the categories of karma, the Tathāgata manifests three wheels of teaching to guide and transform disciples, thereby establishing them as a noble assembly:
first, the wheel of supernatural powers; second, the wheel of reading minds; and third, the wheel of instruction and admonition.

If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, harboring a competitive mind, preach doctrines that contradict the authentic scriptures as a counter-argument, he is able to subdue them and cause them to fall into defeat;
this is the fourth matter.

Through the power of the knowledge of meditative concentration, the Tathāgata thoroughly understands the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of beings and teaches them accordingly, causing them to plant seeds, bring them to maturity, and attain liberation; this is the fifth matter.

This is accomplished through the power of knowledge regarding the faculties and dispositions; the Tathāgata perceives the deviant or correct inclinations of the three classes of sentient beings, and having seen them as they truly are, he eradicates evil desires and increases wholesome desires—this is the sixth matter.
The power of knowing the inclinations of beings is achieved through the power of desire and pleasure;

the Tathāgata perceives three types of sentient beings—the coarse, the middling, and the refined—and causes these three types of persons to enter various Dharma gates according to principle. This is the seventh matter.

The power of knowledge regarding the causal nature of the realms is thereby accomplished: the Tathāgata clearly perceives that the factors of the path leading to transcendence result in the fruit of liberation, while the factors of the obstructing path result in the fruit of saṃsāra; he causes [beings] to extinguish the obstructing path and cultivate the path of transcendence—this is the eighth matter.

This is accomplished through the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of all places; the Tathāgata clearly perceives the events of past lives and speaks of past matters in order to cause sentient beings to give rise to a sense of revulsion and fear.
If one encounters śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who cling to the view of eternalism, one is able to subdue them and cause them to fall into defeat;
this is the ninth matter.

It is accomplished through the power of knowing the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*); the Tathāgata clearly perceives all sentient beings dying here and being born there, and bestows predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) according to the truth.
If śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who cling to the view of annihilationism attempt to challenge him, the Tathāgata is able to subdue them and cause them to fall into defeat;
this is the tenth matter.
It is accomplished through the power of knowledge regarding birth and death (*jāti-maraṇa-jñāna-bala*), whereby the Tathāgata himself knows that his liberation is fully realized and unimpeded.
If arrogant śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, who have not attained arhatship yet claim to have already attained it, can be subdued and forced into defeat;
this is the eleventh matter.

This is accomplished through the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*). The Tathāgata possesses the most supreme skillful means for the sake of benefiting others; if someone were to question the Tathāgata regarding his ten powers, he answers the difficult questions according to reality, resolves their doubts, establishes his own correct teaching, and refutes the false doctrines of others—this is the twelfth matter.

It is accomplished by means of the four fearlessnesses that the Tathāgata’s true teaching exists; among those who are able to practice it, those who do not practice it, and those who both practice and do not practice it, the Tathāgata maintains a mind free from defilement toward these three types of persons—this is the thirteenth matter.

It is accomplished by means of the three foundations of mindfulness; the Tathāgata’s Buddha-eye constantly observes all sentient beings throughout day and night in their states of victory and defeat, rescuing and delivering them—this is the fourteenth matter.
It is accomplished by reason of great compassion; the Tathāgata acts according to his teaching and is able both to act and to teach—this is the fifteenth matter.

It is accomplished by reason of the three qualities of non-protection; the Tathāgata’s performance of beneficial deeds for all sentient beings is entirely complete and without deficiency—this is the sixteenth matter.
Because mindfulness is achieved without forgetfulness, the Tathāgata acts in accordance with principle without error throughout the four modes of deportment; this is the seventeenth matter.
It is accomplished through the eradication of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). The Tathāgata contemplates three kinds of dharmas:

first, those practices that bring benefit; second, those practices that cause diminution; and third, those practices that bring both benefit and diminution. Having set aside the latter two types of dharmas, the Tathāgata proclaims the practice that attains benefit. This eighteenth matter is accomplished by means of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the various unshared dharmas (*āveṇikadharma*).
"Ānanda! You should know such matters concerning the Tathāgata as these! Ānanda!"
In what way are the deeds of the Tathāgata inconceivable? Ānanda!

The deeds of all Tathāgatas are countless and immeasurable; the sentient beings of the world cannot perceive them. Although they rely upon language, these deeds cannot be fully manifested by it; they cannot be shown to others so that they might attain awakening and understanding. They are unimpeded throughout all Buddha-fields; all Tathāgatas accord with equality, transcending the sphere of mental objects and being free from the marks of discrimination. Like space, they are without discrimination, for they are in perfect conformity with the Dharma-realm.

"O sons of good family! For this reason, the Buddha says that the affairs of the Tathāgata are inconceivable. His activity pervades all places, and in all places he is without fault. Following through the realms of the three periods of time, he does not extinguish the nature of the Three Jewels. The Tathāgata abides within these matters; the physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body do not abandon the nature of space, yet he manifests his own body in all buddha-fields. The speech of the Tathāgata is not of the nature of sound, yet he preaches the True Dharma using sounds identical to those of each class of beings. The Tathāgata does not take the mind as an object of perception, yet he thoroughly penetrates the minds, faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of all sentient beings."
"Ānanda! This is called the Tathāgata’s inconceivable activity.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, seventy-five thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas within this great assembly immediately attained the realization and vision of the perfect Dharmakāya; furthermore, seventy-five thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas immediately attained the Mahāyāna Samādhi of Sublime Light; furthermore, seventy-five thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained the patience of non-arising regarding all dharmas; countless asaṃkhyeya sentient beings conceived the non-retrogressive mind toward unsurpassed bodhi; immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings became free from dust and defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye; and furthermore, immeasurable sentient beings attained the superior fruit.

Chapter Six: Praise (Part Two) The Sūtra on the Supreme Reliance, Chapter Six: Praise At that time, Ānanda, having heard the Buddha’s teaching within the great assembly, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness at such an unprecedented experience. Rising from his seat, he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined in reverence, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance. With a pure mind, he spoke these verses in praise:
“Among all sentient beings of the three periods of time, The Tathāgata is most supreme, beyond all comparison.
In the realm of persons and dharmas, he is unequaled; Therefore, he is equanimous toward all.”
That which should be subdued and extinguished has been forever eliminated; that which should be known has been fully mastered.
You are the supreme, the most excellent, and the foremost; O World-Honored Buddha, there is no other like you.

To have power and yet be without fear is true speech; because the Tathāgata possesses power and fearlessness, the World-Honored One’s great capability does not harm others—this is indeed an inconceivable and marvelous matter.
He transforms sentient beings through skillful means; it is not out of a mind of malice or delusion.
When sentient beings are arrogant and self-exalting due to false pride, the World-Honored One subdues them so that they may abandon these traits.
If a person possesses the power to overcome others, this is said to be a verbal transgression in the world;
yet if one points to the Tathāgata, the Most Supreme Honored One, these words are utterly true and free from error.
If anyone should pose correct challenges based on reason, there is none who can cause the Tathāgata to yield;
the Tathāgata is invincible and free from any deficiency, leading sentient beings to the place of ultimate bliss.
The fourfold purity is free from fault; because of these four purities, there is no need for protection.
Possessing the four analytical knowledges, you preach without end; the flavor of the Dharma overflows, satiating all sentient beings.
Possessing unimpeded wisdom regarding the locus of all phenomena, never losing or diminishing any of the foundations of mindfulness,
maintaining great compassion equally toward all sentient beings, and having a mind unstained by worldly dharmas.
Thoroughly penetrating all faculties, desires, and natures, Having already transcended all methods of instruction,
He expounds various gates of remedial means For each distinct category of afflictions.
The World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma is supreme; yet ordinary beings who encounter the Buddha fail to attain understanding.
Enveloped by the darkness of ignorance and delusion, such as these are most difficult to deliver.
The World-Honored One’s fame inspires longing; seeing the Buddha brings inexhaustible joy.
The Buddha’s words can purify the mind; the Great Teacher’s true teaching liberates one from birth and death.
Praising the Buddha can eliminate all inauspiciousness; Recalling the Buddha causes the mind to be ever joyful;
Seeking the Buddha immediately gives rise to Great Prajñā; Understanding the Buddha leads directly to the attainment of the Knowledge of All Modes.
The Tathāgata, through the purity of his precepts, is stainless; The Tathāgata, through the clarity of his meditative mind, is serene;
The Tathāgata, through his wisdom, is immovable; The Dharma-ocean of the Tathāgata is filled with nectar.
While sentient beings slumber in ignorance, the Buddha alone awakens; he surveys everywhere the faculties, natures, and inclinations of all beings.
Though sentient beings are heedless, the Tathāgata is not; he regards all sentient beings with equal vision.
The Buddha has already taught the Dharma for destroying the thieves of the fetters; the Buddha has already eliminated the magical illusions of Māra.
He has shown that birth and death are defects, and he has clarified the fearless realm beyond them.
If there were any dharma that could be measured or bestowed upon others, Just as the World-Honored One practiced great compassion,
Then Devadatta would be supreme, Bestowing bodhi upon all sentient beings.
I am now unable to see the right practice; by cultivating this upholding, I repay the World-Honored One’s kindness.
Even if a person has reached the nirvana without remainder, that person has still not repaid the Buddha’s kindness.
If a person can practice the Buddha’s true path, they are merely cultivating the Dharma for their own benefit;
yet the World-Honored One exhausted himself for the sake of sentient beings—how can one repay such unsurpassed, profound kindness?
The World-Honored One has proclaimed the True Dharma, enabling people to cultivate themselves and transform others;
had the Tathāgata not appeared in this world, only the suffering of sensation would have oppressed their bodies.
The entire world is but a realm of evil paths, where one hears only the great sounds of wailing;
the suffering endured throughout the six realms is no different, for all are entangled and enveloped by afflictions.
The World-Honored One, to untie the fetters of sentient beings, has long been bound by the bonds of great compassion.
The World-Honored One is the unsurpassed field of supreme merit;
those who rely on the Buddha and practice the right path are like me, who never see the exhaustion of good jewels, and it is the same even for those who practice evil deeds.
If one harbors a sense of indifference toward the Buddha, such sentient beings fall into the realm of defeat;
if they suddenly give rise to resentment and contention against the World-Honored One, there is no doubt that they will dwell forever in the darkness.
Just as the Great Teacher recognizes himself, and those similar to the Great Teacher can likewise recognize him,
while others cannot recognize him in this way— I now pay universal homage to the Honored Ones of the ten directions.

The power of all merits and wisdom, the manifested body and the dharma-body of the World-Honored One—out of great compassion, You desire that sentient beings recognize these; therefore, I now prostrate with my head at Your feet.
Exquisite in color and fine in fragrance, one never tires of beholding it; its myriad marks are perfect, surpassing all other forms.
Blooming throughout the three periods of time, it is most deeply beloved—such a Buddha-flower I prostrate before with my head.
The World-Honored One well knows the unsurpassed state, From which all perils and difficulties are transcended;
Without trace, without accumulation, and without artifice— I now prostrate to the Honored One among two-legged beings.
The World-Honored One has washed away all defilements and impurities;
dwelling in the water of the merit of the True Dharma, he has been pure both internally and externally from the very beginning. I now prostrate to this truly pure body.
The World-Honored One is naturally endowed with all wholesome dharmas; He constantly brings profound benefit to the multitudes.
Raining down nectar extensively, he satisfies all sentient beings; I now prostrate to the one who is able to benefit others.
The most supreme person revered by the world—this person still pays homage to the Buddha;
with all evils severed and virtues perfected, I now prostrate to the Most Supreme Honored One.
There is not a single skillful means that you do not cultivate and study, out of compassion for sentient beings whom you wish to deliver;
to lead them across the perilous pit of birth and death, I now prostrate to you, the World’s Refuge.
I prostrate to the incomparable body of wondrous form; I prostrate to the one who can preach the nectar-like Dharma;
I prostrate to the pure wisdom free from defilement; I prostrate to the forest of all virtuous qualities.
Chapter 7: Entrustment (Part II). In the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra*, Chapter Seven, "Entrustment," the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"You should receive, uphold, and maintain this Dharma-gate."
At that time, Ānanda knelt with his right knee on the ground and addressed the Buddha:
“Having now heard this profound Dharma from the Buddha, I have attained what I never had before; I shall receive it upon the crown of my head and uphold it faithfully.”
"Bhagavān, what should this sutra be named?
How should it be upheld?"
The Buddha said,

“Ānanda! This sūtra is named ‘The Supreme Reliance,’ and it is also named ‘The Unprecedented,’ and it is also named ‘The Compendium of Wholesome Dharmas,’ and it is also named ‘Pure Conduct,’ and it is also named ‘The Culmination of Practice.’”
Ānanda! There are ten dharmas for upholding this sutra. What are these ten?

First, copying; second, making offerings; third, transmitting and circulating; fourth, listening attentively; fifth, reading for oneself; sixth, memorizing and upholding; seventh, explaining extensively; eighth, reciting for oneself; ninth, reflecting; and tenth, practicing.
Ānanda! These ten kinds of dharmas can uphold this sutra; they are a true mass of merit, immeasurable and inexhaustible. Ānanda!
Just as wherever the king of wish-fulfilling jewels is located, all manner of precious gems appear;
so it is with one who upholds this sutra—all wholesome dharmas will likewise be accomplished.
Ānanda! Just as all forests and medicinal herbs grow by depending upon the earth,
so too do all wholesome dharmas increase by means of this sutra.
Ānanda! For example, all wholesome dharmas—whether already arisen, currently arising, or yet to arise—are sustained by heedfulness, and thus heedful practice is supreme.
Whether a sutra teaches the Dharma of the śrāvakas, the Dharma of the pratyekabuddhas, or the Dharma of the bodhisattvas, that which is subsumed within this [sutra] is supreme.
Ānanda! Just as when a Wheel-Turning Sage King is in the world, the seven treasures always follow him;
so it is with this sutra: if it remains in the world, the lineage of the Buddha-jewel, the Dharma-jewel, and the Sangha-jewel will continue in succession without interruption.

Ānanda! You should, in turn, extensively expound this sutra for the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, as well as for the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
"Why is this? It is because he wishes to cause all classes of sentient beings to plant roots of goodness toward the Tathāgata.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Ānanda and the great assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, as well as Śakra, the Brahma hosts, the World-Protecting Devas, and others, having heard this rare Dharma-gate spoken by the Buddha, leaped for joy and, with faith and acceptance, put it into practice.
